summary: Defines the Robust XML Encoding Rules (RXER), a set of ASN.1 encoding rules that produce an XML representation of values of any ASN.1 data type. It also defines a canonical form. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers describe data using a strict format. This note turns that data into readable XML tags, always in the same careful way.

questions: how to encode asn.1 as xml
what is the difference between rxer and crxer
why use xml for asn.1 encoding
subtitle: Standard rules to encode ASN.1 data structures as XML, with a canonical form.

tldr.problem: ASN.1 is used to define data structures in protocols, but its existing binary encoding rules (BER) produce opaque, difficult-to-inspect representations that are not human-readable or web-compatible.
tldr.mechanism: RXER defines a set of encoding rules that convert ASN.1 values into XML, making the data readable and exchangeable with XML tools. CRXER further restricts RXER to produce a single canonical form, ensuring that the same data always encodes identically.
tldr.outcome: Developers can now use XML tools and parsers to work with ASN.1-defined data, and cryptographic or comparison operations can rely on canonical CRXER encodings, though the protocol is experimental.

today: RFC 4910 is an Experimental protocol defining XML encoding rules for ASN.1 data. It has not been obsoleted, and developers working with ASN.1-based protocols who need XML interchange or human-readable representations can apply RXER or CRXER (when deterministic encoding is required for cryptographic operations).

sections.title: Introduction to RXER
sections.content:
This RFC defines the Robust XML Encoding Rules (RXER), a set of encoding rules for Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) that produce an XML representation of values of any given ASN.1 data type. RXER allows ASN.1-defined data to be interchanged using XML tools and serialized in a human-readable format.

Unlike existing binary encoding rules such as BER (Basic Encoding Rules), RXER produces XML documents that can be edited, validated, and processed using standard XML tools. The RFC also defines a restriction called CRXER (Canonical RXER) that produces a single unique encoding for any given ASN.1 value, making it suitable for cryptographic operations and data comparison. A pre-existing ASN.1 specification can be used with RXER without modification, though encoding instructions can be added to fine-tune the encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine your data is written in computer shorthand. This document explains how to translate it into English-like tags and text that anyone can read.

sections.title: ASN.1 Types and XML Encoding
sections.content:
ASN.1 defines basic types such as INTEGER, BOOLEAN, OCTET STRING and character strings, as well as combining types like SEQUENCE, SET, SEQUENCE OF, SET OF and CHOICE. In RXER, simple types are encoded as XML text content or attributes, while combining types map to XML elements with child elements or attributes corresponding to their components.

For example, an ASN.1 INTEGER value is encoded as an XML text node containing the integer in decimal form. An ASN.1 BOOLEAN is encoded as true or false. A SEQUENCE type defines multiple named components, each encoded as a child element with the component's name as the element name. A CHOICE type, where only one of several alternatives is present, encodes the chosen alternative as a single element.
sections.plainLanguage: A number becomes 42 in tags. A list of items becomes multiple tags with A and B inside. Each type has its own tag.

sections.title: Fundamental Encoding Rules
sections.content:
RXER specifies how each ASN.1 type converts to XML. An ASN.1 module maps to a target namespace in XML. Named types become XML elements, with element names derived from the ASN.1 identifiers. Attributes within ASN.1 types can encode as XML attributes or child elements, depending on encoding instructions or the type itself.

Special provisions handle restricted character string types (such as IA5String and VisibleString), which encode as text content with characters represented literally. BIT STRING types encode bits as a space-separated list of bit positions or as a hexadecimal string. Time types (GeneralizedTime, UTCTime) encode in their standard string form. OBJECT IDENTIFIER types encode as a dot-separated sequence of numbers. The Markup type (a special ASN.1 type for carrying raw XML) allows raw XML content to be embedded in the encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Each data type has specific rules: numbers as text, true/false as words, lists as multiple tags, dates in standard format, each one consistent.

sections.title: Character Data and Special Encodings
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how different character data types translate to XML text. Restricted character string types (such as PrintableString, IA5String) encode their characters directly in the XML text content. BIT STRING values encode as space-separated decimal bit positions (e.g., 0 2 4) or in hexadecimal form depending on the encoding. OCTET STRING values encode in hexadecimal with optional line breaks.

Floating-point REAL values encode in decimal, hexadecimal, or special values like PLUS-INFINITY and MINUS-INFINITY. When an ASN.1 value uses XML as part of its definition (the Markup type), the XML content is encoded with its attributes and child elements preserved, enabling protocol specifications to embed markup fragments within structured data.
sections.plainLanguage: Text stays as text. Numbers stay as numbers. Binary data becomes hex digits. Special values like infinity get their own words.

sections.title: Canonical RXER (CRXER) Encoding
sections.content:
CRXER is a restriction of RXER that produces a single unique, canonical encoding for any ASN.1 value. Where RXER allows flexibility in element ordering, attribute ordering, or whitespace, CRXER mandates a single deterministic form. For example, CRXER requires elements to appear in a fixed order, attributes to be sorted by name, and whitespace to be normalized.

Canonical encoding is essential for cryptographic operations such as signing or computing digests, because the canonical form is reproducible: the same ASN.1 value always encodes to identical XML bytes. Developers can hash a CRXER encoding and be confident that any other implementation will produce the same hash for the same data. The RFC specifies namespace prefix generation, attribute ordering and element ordering rules to ensure determinism.
sections.plainLanguage: CRXER says: always put things in the same order, always spell words the same way, always line things up the same. This way, two people encoding the same data get identical text they can verify.

sections.title: XML Namespaces and Extensibility
sections.content:
RXER uses XML namespaces to prevent naming conflicts and to organize elements. Each ASN.1 module is assigned a target namespace, and elements defined in that module use the namespace prefix or declaration. The RFC defines how namespace prefixes are generated and assigned in both standard RXER and canonical CRXER forms.

ASN.1 allows extensibility groups in SEQUENCE and SET types, where new components can be added to future versions of the specification. RXER encodes unknown extension components (those not defined in the current specification) with special preservation rules, allowing encoded data to survive round-trip encoding and decoding even when some components are unknown. This supports forward compatibility with new protocol versions.
sections.plainLanguage: Namespaces keep things organized: <mycompany:data> versus <yourcompany:data>. New data formats can be added without breaking old ones.
